one_liner: Rust x86/x86-64 instruction decoder and formatter; in current disas-bench runs it decodes 5-9x faster than XED and Zydis.
what_it_does: Decodes x86-64 (long mode), 32-bit protected mode and 16-bit real mode machine code into a fixed-size, heap-free Instruction struct (opcode, up to four operands, prefixes, immediate, displacement, memory access size). It can also format the instruction as Intel, pseudo-C or (since 2.2.0) MASM-style text. Rust callers use InstDecoder::decode_slice for one-off decodes, or decode_into with a yaxpeax-arch Reader to refill one caller-owned Instruction in a loop. The API is its own and is not Capstone-, XED- or Zydis-compatible. It disassembles; it does not assemble or encode.
how_it_is_fast: Decoding starts from a 256-entry OPCODES table whose records pack the opcode and a 16-bit operand-handling code (bit 15 means 'read ModR/M'). A dedicated hot path handles common unprefixed opcodes before the general prefix/0F/0F38/0F3A loop. The decoder writes into a caller-provided Instruction rather than building a new one, is generic over the reader and annotation sink (the no-op NullSink compiles the annotation code away), and uses inline(always) plus unreachable_unchecked to prune impossible match arms (the CHANGELOG measured about 5% loss without the latter). Formatting writes into a fixed 512-byte InstructionTextBuffer; the author's commit 681262f records display time falling from 91 ns to 47 ns per instruction against 15 ns per decode.
when_to_use: Bulk linear-sweep disassembly of large x86-64 code sections (binary analysis, indexing, gadget search, coverage tooling) where decode throughput dominates.
Rust projects, including no_std or embedded and kernel-adjacent code: the crate builds without std and has no allocation in the decode path.
Decode plus Intel-syntax text output at volume: in the 2025 disas-bench runs its decode+format beat every other library measured, iced included.
Tools that need 16-, 32- and 64-bit decoding behind one interface, or per-microarchitecture decoders (Zen 2 to Zen 5 presets since 2.1.0) that reject instructions a given CPU lacks.
Mixed-architecture tools already using the yaxpeax-arch traits (yaxpeax-arm and the other yaxpeax decoders).
when_not_to_use: C or C++ codebases that want a supported native API. The ffi/ crates have no header files, need nightly cargo (-Z build-std) for the documented build, and the author called them 'kinda useless and awful' in open issue #33 (June 2024). Zydis, XED or bddisasm fit better there.

Encoding or assembling instructions, or rich semantics such as CPU-flag effects and register read/write lists for every instruction: iced re-encodes and carries more semantic data. yaxpeax has had operand access and exception behavior only since 2.1.0 (May 2026).
Non-x86 targets from one library: this crate is x86 only (other yaxpeax crates cover other ISAs separately, unlike Capstone).

Decoders that must reject encodings exactly as hardware does on older crate versions: 2.1.0 to 2.2.0 (2026) fixed many over-permissive VEX/EVEX acceptances, swapped operands, wrong register extensions and wrong memory sizes, so pin 2.2.x or later.
AT&T syntax output: the formats offered are Intel, pseudo-C and MASM-style.

integration.dependencies: yaxpeax-arch 0.3.1, num-traits, cfg-if; serde, serde_derive and serde_json optional (the default features std, colors, use-serde, fmt and behavior pull in serde)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (Cargo.toml has no rust-version; edition 2018). The benchmark runs used rustc 1.52.1 (2021), 1.88.0 and 1.90.0 (2025). The ffi/ build instructions need nightly cargo -Z build-std.
integration.platforms: Any Rust target (no architecture-specific code per the ffi README); decodes x86-16, x86-32 and x86-64 code. The benchmarks ran on x86-64 hosts (i5-6600K, Ryzen 9 9950X, i9-13900K).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; InstDecoder is plain data (two u64 flag words) used through &self, and each decode writes into a caller-owned Instruction, so one Instruction per thread suffices.

gotchas: Release builds rely on unsafe unreachable_unchecked and get_unchecked on hot paths. Earlier releases had reachable panics and an unsoundness: 1.1.2 fixed a debug-build EVEX panic, 1.1.3 fixed out-of-range RegSpec helpers that could print arbitrary const data, and 1.1.4 fixed a reachable unreachable under DisplayStyle::C. The crate is fuzzed with mishegos and in-tree cargo fuzz targets.

The README points to an 'examples directory for FFI usage' that does not exist (issue #33, open since February 2024). The FFI formatter neither returns a length nor guarantees NUL termination, per the author.

Intel-style output prints relative branch targets as $+0xNN unless you use the AbsoluteAddressFormatter or DisplayRules added in 2.2.0, so text output differs from Zydis or XED and diffing against them needs normalization.

The default InstDecoder accepts every extension plus both Intel- and AMD-specific quirks of undefined encodings. Use InstDecoder::minimal() or a uarch preset to reject instructions a target CPU lacks. Cargo.toml at HEAD still says 2.2.0 while the CHANGELOG lists 2.2.1 changes (August 2026 commits), so crates.io's latest is 2.2.0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick yaxpeax-x86 over iced when you want the highest decode and decode+format throughput in Rust, a no_std build and small code size, and you need neither re-encoding nor iced's richer semantics. In the 2025 disas-bench charts it edges iced by about 1.04-1.27x on decode and 1.16-1.24x on decode+format. Pick Zydis, XED or bddisasm instead from C or C++, where yaxpeax's FFI is unfinished, and diStorm only for small pre-AVX2 C use.
verified_claims_summary: The catalogued numbers come from icedland/disas-bench (June 2021, i5-6600K, rustc 1.52.1, gcc 10.3.0 LTO builds, one linear sweep per library over Firefox 86 xul.dll .text): yaxpeax decoded at 182.08 MB/s against Zydis 34.19 and XED 55.39, but its decode+format (40.05 MB/s) trailed iced and diStorm. The newer athre0z/disas-bench charts (October 2025, yaxpeax-x86 submodule 681262f, 2.0-era, after the formatting optimization; 20 passes over 0x2460400 bytes) reverse that. On athre0z's own i9-13900K run (GCC 14.2, rustc 1.90.0) yaxpeax decode is about 406 MB/s against iced 390, XED 73 and Zydis full 57, and decode+format about 192 against iced 165, diStorm 94 and Capstone 26. On iximeow's Ryzen 9 9950X run (GCC 13.3, rustc 1.88.0) decode is about 462 against iced 363 and XED 67, and decode+format about 198 against iced 160 and Capstone 28 (bar lengths measured in pixels against the axis ticks, derived from page data).
status_note: Actively maintained (2.1.0 to 2.2.0 released May-July 2026, last commit 2026-08-08) and 0BSD-licensed, so it is copyable. No harness flaw was found in the drivers. However, the catalogued 2021 numbers are stale: they predate the formatting rework that now puts yaxpeax ahead of iced on decode+format. The Ryzen 9950X chart was produced by yaxpeax's own author (PR #16), so only the i9-13900K run is third-party. Neither run measured the 2026 releases, whose stricter VEX/EVEX rejection and new behavior data are unbenchmarked. The disas-bench drivers count instructions but never read the decoded fields, which is the same for every library.
